subject: Biology
title: Mitosis: Copying the Blueprint
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Mitosis: Copying the Blueprint.

hook.text: When a cell divides by mitosis, it creates two identical copies of itself.

buildup.text: First, every chromosome is duplicated. Then the cell pulls copies to opposite sides.

discovery.text: Four phases drive the process: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase.

twist.text: Plant cells can't pinch apart like animal cells. They build a new wall down the middle.

climax.text: Mitosis replaces your skin, blood, and tissue with perfect genetic copies every day.

punchline.text: Two cells. Same DNA. Perfect copies.

details.summary: Mitosis is the process of cell division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell. It occurs in four stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, ensuring each new cell receives a complete copy of all 46 chromosomes.
details.whyItMatters: Mitosis is how organisms grow, repair damaged tissues, and maintain themselves throughout life. Errors in mitosis can lead to cells with wrong chromosome numbers, which can cause developmental problems or cancer.
takeaways: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells
Chromosomes are replicated and then separated into each new cell
The cell cycle includes checkpoints that verify DNA integrity

faq.question: What are the four stages of mitosis?
faq.answer: In prophase, chromosomes condense and become visible. In metaphase, they line up along the cell's center. In anaphase, sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. In telophase, nuclear membranes reform around each chromosome set and the cell divides.

faq.question: How often do human cells divide through mitosis?
faq.answer: It varies enormously by cell type. Skin and gut lining cells divide every few days. Liver cells divide rarely unless damaged. Neurons and muscle cells almost never divide in adults. The body performs roughly 3.8 million cell divisions per second on average.
